title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 9-10
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 9 to 10 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'ईश्वरो विक्रमी धन्वी मेधावी विक्रमः क्रमः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 9 to 10 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 9 to 10.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 9 to 10** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **ईश्वरो विक्रमी धन्वी मेधावी विक्रमः क्रमः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**ईश्वरो विक्रमी धन्वी मेधावी विक्रमः क्रमः । अनुत्तमो दुराधर्षः कृतज्ञः कृतिर् आत्मवान् ॥** **सुरेशः शरणं शर्म विश्वरेताः प्रजाभवः । अहः संवत्सरो व्यालः प्रत्ययः सर्वदर्शनः ॥**

The Lord, the mighty one, the bowman, the wise is he. None is greater than him and none can conquer him. He knows all our deeds, and that God of gods is full of the Self. The Lord even of the gods, our refuge and our joy, is he. The seed of this universe is that Supreme Self. He is the Time that turns the days and years, and he sees everything.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 9 to 10 mean?
faq.a: The Lord, the mighty one, the bowman, the wise is he. None is greater than him and none can conquer him. He knows all our deeds, and that God of gods is full of the Self. The Lord even of the gods, our refuge and our joy, is he. The seed of this universe is that Supreme Self. He is the Time that turns the days and years, and he sees everything.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
